summary: Defines OSPFv2 Opaque LSAs using TLV structures to attach more attributes to prefixes or links. They are optional and backward compatible, and go beyond the fixed-format LSAs of RFC 2328.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7684 adds two optional OSPFv2 LSA formats for attaching attributes to prefixes and links. Their TLV structure makes room for extensions while allowing routers that do not support them to continue operating.

subtitle: Optional TLV-based OSPFv2 LSAs for advertising additional attributes about prefixes and links.

tldr.problem: OSPFv2's fixed-format LSAs do not readily carry new attributes for prefixes and links.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines Extended Prefix and Extended Link Opaque LSAs whose bodies contain Type-Length-Value structures and optional nested sub-TLVs.
tldr.outcome: The new LSAs are optional and backward compatible. This RFC defines the framework and top-level TLVs; other specifications define the additional attributes.

today: RFC 7684 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2015. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why OSPFv2 Needs Extended LSAs
sections.content:
OSPFv2 advertises routing information in fixed-format Link State Advertisements (LSAs), as defined in RFC 2328. These formats do not readily support all new information needed by applications such as source/destination routing, route tagging, and segment routing.

RFC 7684 defines two Opaque LSAs based on Type-Length-Value (TLV) tuples. They associate additional attributes with prefixes or links, whether or not those prefixes or links also appear in fixed-format LSAs. The extensions are optional and backward compatible.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPFv2's existing LSA formats are difficult to extend with new information. This RFC defines optional TLV-based LSAs for adding attributes to prefixes and links.

sections.title: TLVs and Opaque Identifiers
sections.content:
Each TLV has a 16-bit Type, a 16-bit Length, and a value. Length counts only the value, in octets. The TLV and any nested sub-TLVs are padded with zeros to 4-octet alignment; padding is not included in Length. For example, a 3-octet value has Length 3 but occupies 8 octets including its header and padding.

The Opaque ID distinguishes multiple Opaque LSAs of the same kind from one router; it has no other meaning. If several LSAs from that router advertise the same prefix or link, receivers use the attributes from the LSA with the lowest Opaque ID.
sections.plainLanguage: A TLV carries a type, the length of its value, and the value. Zero padding aligns the entries, while the length field excludes that padding.

sections.title: The Extended Prefix Opaque LSA
sections.content:
The Extended Prefix Opaque LSA uses Opaque Type 7. It carries additional attributes for prefixes from Router-LSAs, Network-LSAs, Summary-LSAs, NSSA-LSAs, and AS-external-LSAs. Its LS Type may be 10 for area-local flooding or 11 for AS-wide flooding. The advertising router selects the scope, which must meet the needs of every prefix in that LSA.

The Extended Prefix TLV has type 1 and contains a route type, prefix length, address family, flags, address prefix, and optional sub-TLVs. Route types 0, 1, 3, 5, and 7 mean unspecified, intra-area, inter-area, AS external, and NSSA external. Address-family value 0 currently means IPv4 unicast. The A-Flag identifies an attached inter-area prefix; the N-Flag marks a host prefix identifying the advertising router.

If the same prefix appears more than once in one LSA, receivers use the first instance. When it appears in separate LSAs from the same router, they use the one with the lowest Opaque ID.
sections.plainLanguage: The Extended Prefix LSA attaches route attributes to a prefix. Its TLV identifies the prefix, its route type, and optional flags or further attributes.

sections.title: The Extended Link Opaque LSA
sections.content:
The Extended Link Opaque LSA uses Opaque Type 8 and LS Type 10, so it is flooded within an area. It advertises extra attributes for links in Router-LSAs. Its Extended Link TLV has type 1 and identifies one link using its Link Type, Link ID, and Link Data, followed by sub-TLVs.

Only one Extended Link TLV SHALL appear in each Extended Link Opaque LSA. This allows a change to one link to be advertised separately. Sub-TLVs may appear in any order. The RFC defines the framework, but its sub-TLV registries begin with only a Reserved value; later specifications define actual link and prefix attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: An Extended Link LSA describes one link and its optional attributes. Keeping one link in each LSA lets a router update that link separately.

sections.title: Duplicate and Malformed Information
sections.content:
If a prefix appears multiple times in one Extended Prefix LSA, receivers use only its first instance and SHOULD log an error. If duplicate prefix information appears in separate LSAs from the same router, receivers use the instance in the LSA with the lowest Opaque ID. When different routers advertise a prefix, the application using the information decides which to prefer.

A malformed LSA is one whose TLV or sub-TLV extends beyond its containing data, or leaves too little data for a TLV header. Malformed LSAs MUST NOT be stored in the link-state database, acknowledged, or reflooded. Their reception SHOULD be counted or logged.
sections.plainLanguage: When a prefix is repeated, receivers follow defined rules to choose which entry to use. An LSA with a truncated or overlong TLV is discarded rather than stored or forwarded.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
Opaque LSAs are optional and backward compatible, so routers that do not understand these extensions can continue to operate. Future applications using the extensions MUST define how their own functionality remains backward compatible.

The new LSAs have the same security concerns as OSPFv2 and Opaque LSAs. Applications using them must describe their own security considerations. Implementations must detect malformed TLV combinations so they cannot crash the router or its routing process.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can ignore these optional LSAs without changing their existing operation. Implementations must also handle malformed TLVs without crashing.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA registers Opaque Type 7 for Extended Prefix LSAs and Opaque Type 8 for Extended Link LSAs. The RFC also creates registries for top-level TLVs, sub-TLVs, and Extended Prefix TLV flags.

New TLV values are allocated by IETF Review or IESG Approval. Types from 32768 through 33023 are for experimental use and MUST NOT be mentioned by RFCs. Types from 33024 through 65535 are not assigned until an IETF specification covers the range.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps registries for the new LSA and TLV types. Some values are reserved for experiments, and another range cannot be assigned until an IETF specification defines how to use it.
